title: Iran war to blame for inflation: PM
full_text:
Anthony Albanese insists the war in Iran is to blame for rising interest rates in contravention of the assessment of RBA governor Michele Bullock, amid warnings from the bank that the data centre rollout may fuel inflation and keep rates elevated.
More than halfway through his second term in office, the Prime Minister is under increasing pressure to lift the speed limit of the Australian economy and take the heat out of inflation, which has sat above target for 13 out of 17 quarters under his leadership.
Unsatisfied with Ms Bullock’s assessment that domestic inflationary pressures had forced the bank to hike rates for a fifth time this year, Mr Albanese on Monday instead pointed to comments from the Bank of England, who blamed war in Iran for rising rates.
“On February 28, a war started in Iran that has had an impact on global inflation. We have seen inflation rise around the world. We saw last week interest rates increase, not just in Australia but the Bank of England for the first time in a long while,” Mr Albanese said in Canberra.
“The governor of the central bank there made it very clear what the reason for that was and suggested that if the war in Iran and that conflict was not ended, there would be further pressure on (rates).”
TAD-2789 Inflation (Part 1)
Ms Bullock last week confirmed the monetary policy board’s decision to raise rates to their highest level in 18 years was not from the Iran war-driven oil shock but was aimed at addressing “domestic capacity pressures”.
NSW Treasurer Daniel Moohkey has predicted a “pretty sudden fall” in economic activities after the RBA hiked the interest rate for the fifth time over the past 12 months, particularly among mortgage holders in NSW.
When pressed on his government’s record on inflation and signs Labor was losing the trust of the Australian public, Mr Albanese said he had presided over the lowest average unemployment rate in 50 years and consistently positive growth during “difficult global times”.
TAD-2789 Inflation (Part 2)
He also said inflation was now lower than when his government first came to office in the wake of a global pandemic, and that the government had “produced savings in every single budget”.
Since the then-RBA governor Bernie Fraser announced the bank’s target band of 2-3 per cent in March 1993, Labor under Mr Albanese has been the only government to record average CPI outside the band.
Analysis by The Australian of quarterly CPI data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows inflation has averaged 4.2 per cent under the Albanese government, compared with 2 per cent across the Abbott-Turnbull-Morrison government, 2.5 per cent during the Howard government, 2.7 per cent in the Rudd-Gillard-Rudd years and fractionally under 3 per cent in the final years of the Keating government.
While inflation has been above target for 13 of the 17 quarters under the Albanese government (76 per cent), the Howard government recorded 12 out of 47 (26 per cent), which included four affected by the introduction of the GST.
The Rudd-Gillard-Rudd government oversaw seven above-target inflation quarters out of 23 (30 per cent) and the Abbott-Turnbull-Morrison government four out of 35 (11 per cent), all either towards the end of the Covid pandemic or just after it.
After ANZ released its annual results, chief executive Nuno Matos said despite the short-term pain, it was in Australia’s “best long-term” interest to bring inflation down.
“Low and middle income earnings … are hit the most from inflation,” Mr Matos told The Australian
“The fact that you have inflation and high interest rates is a double impact.
“People have to pay more for their basic needs, and they have to pay more for their mortgage payments. It’s not a great situation.
“Once inflation becomes entrenched, that’s dangerous”.
The previous Coalition government had the lowest proportion of quarters with CPI above the target band of any government since 1993 and presided over above-target inflation only as the Covid pandemic ended and immediately after.
Mr Albanese’s defence of Labor’s economic record coincided with an address by RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter, who warned that surging data centre investment was likely to fuel inflation in the near term.
Noting a 10-fold increase in data centre investment over the past three years, Dr Hunter flagged that the boom was likely to add to inflationary pressures in the near term, though she said AI was likely to be inflation-neutral in the long run as a result of productivity dividends.
“Surging global AI-related investment has contributed to capacity pressures in supply chains for AI-enabling products such as semiconductors,” Dr Hunter told a UBS conference in Sydney.
“These upstream cost pressures are passing through to the prices of some downstream goods in advanced economies.”
